slice_results.behavior_summary: At import-time, the code defines a LiquidParameters class that performs complex mathematical interpolations and calculations related to liquid properties such as specific heat capacity, freezing temperature, density, kinematic viscosity, Reynolds number, and tube pressure drop. It accesses no external data, network, file, or system APIs, and contains no hardcoded IPs, URLs, shell commands, or environment variables. The code purely performs internal numeric computations without any security-sensitive operations or data exfiltration, resulting in no security impact.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code defines a LiquidParameters class that performs purely mathematical computations related to liquid properties such as specific heat capacity, freezing temperature, density, kinematic viscosity, Reynolds number, and tube pressure drop. It does not perform any network operations, dynamic imports, code execution, or system manipulation. There are no obfuscated payloads, no environment variable tampering, no data collection or exfiltration attempts, and no suspicious runtime behavior. Compared to the known malicious patterns, this code lacks any indicators of malware such as dynamic imports of suspicious packages, eval-based payload execution, or system data harvesting. The code is a straightforward scientific computation module with no side effects or security-sensitive operations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or during package initialization, the code dynamically imports and executes a secondary npm package (2e6d5f64604be31), which acts as a crypto drainer, enabling further malicious actions such as wallet draining and unauthorized asset transfers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code dynamically downloads and executes an unlisted, suspiciously named secondary package at runtime, a common technique for evading static analysis and delivering malware payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not download or execute arbitrary code from external, unvetted sources at runtime, especially without user awareness or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Dynamic imports are used in legitimate plugin systems, but only from trusted, well-known sources and never for unlisted or obfuscated packages.
key_indicators: Dynamic import of a non-standard, suspiciously named package (2e6d5f64604be31)
No user notification or consent for code execution
Obfuscation of malicious payload delivery via secondary package
Presence of code that enables further malicious actions after import

execution_context.file_location: main application code (in @ledgerhq/connect-kit v1.1.5 and v1.1.6)

package_info.why_malicious: Versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, and 1.1.7 of @ledgerhq/connect-kit were compromised to include or download crypto drainer malware. The malicious code is designed to either directly or indirectly execute unauthorized transactions, stealing cryptocurrency from users' wallets. The attack is triggered during normal application use, presenting fake wallet connection prompts and exfiltrating assets to attacker-controlled wallets without user consent.

attack_chain.action: Malicious versions of @ledgerhq/connect-kit are published to npm and included as dependencies in target applications.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is distributed to end-user applications via dependency installation.

attack_chain.action: When the application loads the compromised package, malicious code is executed either at import-time or during user interaction.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is presented with a fake wallet connection modal or a secondary drainer package is loaded and executed.

attack_chain.action: User interacts with the fake modal and connects their wallet, or the secondary drainer package initializes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware initiates unauthorized transactions using the connected wallet.

attack_chain.action: Malware drains funds from the connected wallet to attacker-controlled addresses.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen cryptocurrency, achieving the final objective of the attack.

behavioral_signatures: Display of unexpected or suspicious wallet connection modals in applications using @ledgerhq/connect-kit
Automatic initiation of wallet transactions without explicit user consent or confirmation
Dynamic import or download of secondary npm packages (such as 2e6d5f64604be31) at runtime
Execution of code that interacts with browser wallet APIs outside of normal user-initiated flows
file_indicators: Presence of @ledgerhq/connect-kit versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, or 1.1.7 in package.json, package-lock.json, or yarn.lock
References to package 2e6d5f64604be31 in source code or dependency trees
Unexpected changes or additions to node_modules/@ledgerhq/connect-kit/main.js or related files
network_indicators: Outbound cryptocurrency transactions to known attacker wallet addresses immediately following wallet connection events
Unexpected network requests initiated during or after wallet connection flows
Connections to domains or endpoints associated with the secondary drainer package
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor dependency manifests (package.json, lockfiles) for the use of @ledgerhq/connect-kit versions 1.1.5, 1.1.6, or 1.1.7. Analyze application runtime for the presence of fake wallet connection modals and any unauthorized transaction initiations. Flag any dynamic imports or downloads of unlisted npm packages, especially those matching suspicious patterns (e.g., 2e6d5f64604be31). Monitor for network activity involving known attacker wallet addresses or suspicious transaction patterns immediately following wallet connection events. Review source code and built artifacts for references to secondary drainer packages or unexpected modifications to wallet connection logic.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when rsh.js is executed as a detached process, the code collects detailed system, environment, and user information, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload from a base64 string, sets the NODE_NO_EVAL environment variable to undefined, and executes the decompressed payload using eval, resulting in the execution of further malicious code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting extensive system, environment, and user data, compressing and encoding it, and executing obfuscated code via eval are all strong indicators of malicious intent and are commonly used to evade detection and enable data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and exfiltrate system or user information, nor do they execute dynamically decompressed and obfuscated code via eval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression and system info gathering may be used in legitimate diagnostics or telemetry, but not in combination with obfuscated payload execution and without user consent.
key_indicators: Obfuscated and base64-encoded payload decompressed and executed via eval
Systematic collection of system, environment, and user data
Manipulation of environment variables to bypass security controls
No user notification or consent for data collection or code execution

package_info.why_malicious: All packages in this campaign execute obfuscated JavaScript code at install time, which collects extensive system, environment, and user information and establishes a persistent reverse shell to a remote attacker-controlled server (rsh.51pwn.com:8880), enabling full remote code execution and exfiltration of sensitive data. The attack chain is triggered via multiple npm lifecycle hooks, uses detached background processes for persistence, and employs obfuscation and dynamic code execution to evade detection.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering preinstall, postinstall, test, or init scripts defined in package.json.
scripts/init.js is executed, which launches scripts/rsh.js as a detached child process and immediately exits to conceal ongoing activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of scripts/rsh.js in the background

attack_chain.action: scripts/rsh.js collects detailed system, environment, and user data, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload, and executes it via eval.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of reverse shell payload from decompressed code

attack_chain.action: The reverse shell payload establishes a persistent connection to rsh.51pwn.com:8880, exfiltrates collected system information, and provides the attacker with remote shell access for arbitrary command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access and control over the compromised system

behavioral_signatures: Execution of scripts/init.js during npm install, test, or init lifecycle events
Creation of detached child processes in install/test scripts (child_process.fork with {detached: true})
Presence of obfuscated or base64-encoded JavaScript payloads in package files
Use of eval to execute dynamically decompressed or generated code
Outbound TCP connections to hardcoded C2 domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com:8880) during or after installation
Collection and exfiltration of system, environment, and user data during package installation or execution
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript with base64-encoded or Unicode-escaped payloads
network_indicators: Outbound TCP connections to rsh.51pwn.com on port 8880
Initial data exfiltration containing compressed system information
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for execution of scripts during install, test, or init lifecycle events, especially those launching detached child processes or containing obfuscated/base64-encoded code. Flag any package that establishes outbound TCP connections to suspicious domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com) or uncommon ports during or after installation. Use static analysis to detect eval usage on dynamically decompressed payloads and the presence of Unicode-escaped or base64-encoded code. Alert on collection and exfiltration of system, environment, or user data during package installation or execution. Correlate file indicators (scripts/init.js, scripts/rsh.js, suspicious package.json scripts) with behavioral and network indicators for high-confidence detection.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code defines the module as an ES module and exports a null default value, resulting in no data processing or side effects.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is not inherently malicious, but the presence of a package with a single-character name and no functional code is highly unusual. Such packages are often created unintentionally due to typographical errors and can be abused in the future if the code is updated to include malicious payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages typically provide useful functionality or utilities, whereas this package exports only a null value and performs no operations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Test, placeholder, or namespace-reserving packages may sometimes be published with minimal or no functionality, but these are usually clearly marked or not widely downloaded.
key_indicators: Single-character package name ('-')
index.js exports only null as default
No functional code or logic present
Unusually high download count for a non-functional package

package_info.why_malicious: The package '-' is not currently malicious, but its existence and high download count are due to accidental installations caused by typographical errors in npm commands. Its presence in projects is unintentional and could be abused in the future if the package contents change to include malicious code. The risk is that such packages can be silently included in builds, creating a potential supply chain attack vector by providing an opportunity for attackers to later introduce malicious payloads into a widely distributed, trusted dependency.

attack_chain.action: Accidental installation of the '-' package due to typographical errors in npm commands or package.json dependencies.
attack_chain.leads_to: The package is included in the project, potentially as a placeholder for future malicious code, creating a supply chain risk if the package contents are updated with malicious payloads.

behavioral_signatures: Presence of single-character or command-like package names in dependencies (e.g., '-', 'i', 'g', 'D')
Packages with no functional code or only skeleton code (e.g., exporting null or empty modules)
High download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation
file_indicators: package.json dependencies including '-', 'i', 'g', 'D', or other single-character/command-like names
index.js file that only exports null or an empty module
package.json scripts section with non-functional or placeholder scripts referencing missing files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan package.json and package-lock.json for dependencies with suspicious names such as '-', 'i', 'g', or names matching npm command flags. Flag packages that have no functional code or only export null/empty modules in their main files. Check for non-functional npm scripts referencing missing files. Monitor for sudden inclusion of such packages in projects, especially if not explicitly added by developers, and alert on high download counts for packages with no legitimate usage or documentation.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code collects all environment variables, checks for sandbox indicators, and if not detected, sends the environment data via HTTP POST to a hardcoded attacker-controlled domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive credentials and secrets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses all environment variables and exfiltrates them to an external, attacker-controlled domain using an HTTP POST request. The use of base64 encoding and obfuscated domain construction, combined with sandbox evasion logic, is characteristic of credential theft and data exfiltration malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate package code should not access or transmit all environment variables, nor should it communicate with external domains without explicit user consent and clear documentation. Exfiltrating sensitive data to an untrusted domain is a direct violation of user trust and security best practices.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate telemetry or crash reporting tools may send limited, non-sensitive environment data to trusted domains, but they never transmit full environment dumps or send data to untrusted or obfuscated domains.
key_indicators: Access to process.env (all environment variables)
HTTP POST request to a hardcoded, attacker-controlled domain
Base64 encoding of environment data prior to transmission
Obfuscated domain construction using array joins
Conditional execution based on sandbox detection

package_info.why_malicious: Multiple versions of the package contain code that collects all environment variables from the victim machine and exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook using HTTP POST requests. The code employs sandbox and analysis environment detection to evade automated security scanners. The latest version (0.1.0) is benign, likely to avoid detection by scanners that only analyze the most recent release.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed as a dependency due to dependency confusion and unpinned versioning.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code execution on victim machine

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that access and exfiltrate environment variables, especially those making HTTP POST requests to known malicious domains such as pipedream.net subdomains. Flag packages containing large environment variable filter lists or obfuscated code in build.js or similar files. Pay special attention to packages with multiple high-numbered versions and a benign latest version, as this is a common evasion technique. Use both static and dynamic analysis to inspect all package versions, not just the latest, and correlate network activity with package installation or import events.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time, the code collects detailed system and environment information (CPU details, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers, and package metadata), serializes it, and sends it via HTTPS POST to an external domain, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive host data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code gathers sensitive system and environment information and exfiltrates it to an external, attacker-controlled domain without user knowledge or consent. This enables reconnaissance of internal environments and can facilitate further targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and transmit host or environment information on import, especially to untrusted domains, and always require user consent for telemetry.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics or error reporting packages may collect limited telemetry, but this is always documented, opt-in, and never includes sensitive host details like usernames or DNS servers.
key_indicators: Collection of sensitive system and environment data (CPU, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers)
Network exfiltration via HTTPS POST to non-standard domain (oast.pro)
No user notification or consent for data collection or transmission
Presence of code referencing os, dns, and process environment in package entry point

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are proof-of-concept (PoC) dependency confusion attacks that attempt to exfiltrate system information or download and execute code from external servers. While no outright malicious payload is present, the behavior is consistent with supply chain attack techniques and poses a risk to internal systems if installed. The packages make unsolicited network requests during installation or import, which can be used to confirm internal usage or leak sensitive environment data.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed via dependency confusion, replacing or supplementing an internal package with an attacker-controlled version.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of postinstall or import-time code embedded in the malicious package

attack_chain.action: Malicious code executes during installation or import, performing network beaconing or exfiltrating system information to external servers.

attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: enable further targeted attacks or demonstrate internal exposure

Collection and exfiltration of system environment data (CPU, home directory, hostname, username, DNS servers) at import-time

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that initiate network requests to external or non-standard domains during installation (postinstall) or import. Use static analysis to flag packages whose entry points (e.g., app.js, index.js) reference os, dns, or process environment modules and contain code for network exfiltration. Block or alert on packages with postinstall scripts or code that contacts external servers using the package name. Inspect network logs for HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains such as *.lupin.com and *.oast.pro, especially if requests contain serialized system or environment data.
